surfaces.part: leaf crown top (lit upper clusters, rounded dome-like mass)
crown front/underside (dark shaded foliage and shadow under crown)
root flare and grass tufts at base

answer.evidence: The crown is the main volume. Its width profile widens from 2 px at row 1 to 44 px at rows 18-20, then narrows to 24 px at row 43 and 10 px at the trunk. That gives a rounded, ellipse-like mass. Rows 4-20 hold the lighter, sunlit leaf clusters (#538b42, #6fa95a) that read as the upper surface of the crown. Rows 21-45 are darker foliage (#2d5b34), with near-black shadow at rows 38-45 where the crown overhangs the trunk, and these form the front face. The trunk (rows 46-58, brown) and the root flare with grass (rows 57-63) add roughly 13-18 more rows of front. There is no hard front-edge line, so the top evidence is the volumetric lit-top and dark-underside shading plus the ellipse-like silhouette. A tree crown is a organic blob, not a flat slab, and not a flat front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate canopy is a rounded mass with only about 4 green steps and soft, blurry clumps. It lacks the crisp per-leaf clusters and bright highlight leaves seen in both references. The trunk is a plain brown shape with little bark grain or root flare, whereas the references have detailed roots and branches visible through the canopy. Measured visible tones per tile are 8 against 26-29 for the references, which is far lower, and the raw colour count (25 total vs 427-567) agrees. Outlines are tinted dark green and brown with 0% neutral edge pixels, so they are not near-black. There are no flat fills (0% near-flat coverage). Overall the tree is clean but noticeably thinner and flatter than the Beodeul standard, so it fails on density and shading depth.
